title: Remember when NASA slammed a spacecraft into an asteroid? We now have close-up images of the aftermath

blocks.text: Science·New

Four years after NASA slammed a spacecraft into an asteroid to see if it could successfully alter its orbit around a larger companion, the European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has arrived to see just how well that went.
'It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to finally see what happened,' says Hera mission scientist
In 2021, NASA embarked on an ambitious mission: Sending a spacecraft to slam into one of two asteroids in a double-asteroid system to test whether the impact could change its orbit.
Why? To see if the technology could be used to redirect any potentially hazardous asteroid that was on a collision course with Earth. (Don’t panic: There’s no known asteroid on a collision course.)

The binary asteroid system consists of Didymos and its smaller moonlet, Dimorphos, which orbit a common centre of mass. The mission was to slam into the moonlet to see if it would change its orbit around Didymos.

Fast forward to September 2022, and the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) did just that. It shortened Dimorphos's orbit around Didymos by roughly 33 minutes. NASA had anticipated a change of roughly 10 minutes.
While telescopes on Earth revealed the aftermath, another mission — the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Hera — was planned to take a closer look.
Now, ESA has released close-up images and videos of the pair four years after DART.
Looking closely at the images and video, there is a noticeable flattening on Dimorphos compared to pre-impact.

“But now where that rounded face was, now, well, it's a big crater … that is almost as large as the body itself, which is really, really spectacular,” said Sabina Raducan, planetary scientist with the International Space Science Institute and part of the Hera mission.
“It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to finally see what happened.”
A big surprise
But there was more for Hera to discover.

“Every space mission has surprises. But there was a particularly big one in store for Hera,” said Naomi Murdoch, planetary scientist with ISAE-SUPAERO at the Université de Toulouse, and part of the Hera science team.
“Hera has observed hundreds of boulders moving around these two asteroids and ranging in size from tens of centimetres to metre-sized,” she said.
The image produced by 11 long-exposure images look like fireflies are swarming around the pair of asteroids.

This is a composite image combining 11 long-exposure Hyperscout H images, centred on the Didymos asteroid. The dot trails correspond to hundreds of boulders of differing sizes in motion around the Didymos-Dimorphos system. The two asteroids have been subtracted from the image for improved visualisation of the boulders. These images were acquired on 6 November with an approximate distance of 29.9 km from the asteroids. (European Space Agency)
But it’s not clear from where they originated. Was it a result of the 2022 impact, or were they there before, as part of Didymos?

“We're still really trying to characterize them,” Murdoch said. “So, understanding with lots of imaging what their sizes are and how exactly they're moving in the space around the asteroids. So right now, we're not entirely sure where they came from.”
Hera has been orbiting the dual asteroid system for the past three weeks. There are still six months left in its mission. And scientists are eager to discover more.

Comparing images of the Didymos system before and after the 2022 impact of NASA's DART mission with the smaller Dimorphos moonlet. The left-side image is a view from the DART spacecraft shortly before impact. The right-side image is a view from Hera, aiming to match the previous mission's view angle as closely as possible. Dimorphos appears entirely transformed, with its once-rounded face flattened into a crater that seems as wide as the impacted face of the asteroid and some weird structures inside it, including an apparent cigar-shaped structure at its centre. (NASA/Johns Hopkins APL/European Space Agency)
For example, Didymos looks like a giant walnut, with a pronounced ridge across the 700-metre wide asteroid.

“The central ridge is a very spectacular feature of this asteroid. What we know is that the asteroid is rotating very fast, and we think that what happens when asteroids rotate fast is that the material on the surface actually flows down from the higher latitudes, down towards the equatorial region,” Murdoch explained.

blocks.text: Another interesting thing is that, since the impact, Dimorphos is now tumbling as it orbits.
“Before the DART impact, Dimorphos was more like our own moon. So it was always showing the same face to Didymos,” Raducan said. “It was behaving quite nicely. Now it's very chaotic.”
More successful than anticipated
Not only did DART change Dimorphos’s orbit around Didymos, but it turns out it also changed the pair’s orbit around the sun.

In March, a study published in the journal Science Advances, reported that the impact changed its 770-day orbital period around the sun by a fraction of a second. A fraction of a second may not seem like much, but it marks the first time in history that a human-made object has changed the orbit of an object around the sun.
NASA slams spacecraft into asteroid to test planetary defence

Over the next six months, Hera will continue to collect data about the binary asteroid system to see what else may have changed. It will deploy two CubeSats (miniature satellites), to further explore both the mineral make-up of Dimorphos as well as the first radar sounding within an asteroid.
After that, the pair will descend to the asteroid’s surface. And when Hera’s mission is completed, it too will descend to the surface.

For now, astronomers are excited to see what the next six months will tell them about this little pairing, and specifically, if an asteroid re-direct mission is a viable solution to keeping Earth safe.

“We learned that from DART, that we can send a spacecraft there, we can hit it, and now from Hera, we can see this effect,” Raducan said. “We know that we can deflect it. The next question that we would need to answer as we get more data is to see how much this deflection, how efficient this deflection actually was.”

Based in Toronto, Nicole covers all things science for CBC News. As an amateur astronomer, Nicole can be found looking up at the night sky appreciating the marvels of our universe. She is the editor of the Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada and the author of several books.
